target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly good for society because it improves convenience, productivity, accessibility, and workplace safety
objection: AI instead harms important social goods: it damages economic well-being for many people and businesses, weakens critical thinking in students and adults, entrenches racism against racial minorities, and creates dangerous privacy risks. On that basis, AG2 argues AI is not good for society.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is not good for society because of privacy and racial-bias harms
objection: Privacy and bias risks are not inevitable; AI can be deployed with data minimization, encryption/access controls, human oversight, and auditing to reduce privacy risk and mitigate biased outcomes. AG1 also rejects the idea that society must require zero harm, arguing AI can still be good if benefits are material and harms are controllable.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy and racial-bias harms can be sufficiently controlled by safeguards and that some harm is acceptable if benefits are large
objection: Health- and data-intensive AI systems require collecting, linking, and processing large amounts of sensitive personal data, so privacy vulnerabilities persist despite encryption or access controls. In addition, racial bias comes from biased training data and real-world generalization, and audits or human oversight cannot guarantee elimination of those biases across future uses and contexts.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy and racial-bias harms are structurally persistent and not controllable
objection: Many AI applications can be built with privacy-preserving architectures such as on-device inference, federated learning, and differential-privacy-style methods, so they do not inherently require continuous collection and linking of sensitive data. Racial disparities are also not fixed: fairness-aware training, evaluation, and deployment corrections can substantially reduce unequal outcomes.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s benefits outweigh the concern that it may weaken critical thinking
objection: AI use in tutoring, drafting, and analysis can cause cognitive offloading: it gives polished outputs that reduce users’ incentives to independently reason, evaluate evidence, and check their work. Because critical thinking is a core societal good, materially weakening it makes AI not good for society.

target: AG2’s claim that AI tutoring inherently weakens critical thinking through cognitive offloading
objection: AI tutoring can be designed to prompt learners through problems, check steps, and give targeted explanations rather than simply supplying finished answers. When learners repeatedly practice reasoning with feedback and prompts to verify evidence, their critical thinking can improve rather than decline.

target: AG1’s claim that AI tutoring can improve critical thinking because it provides guided learning
objection: In practice, AI tutors often look authoritative, so learners defer to them instead of independently evaluating reasoning and evidence. Also, verifying AI feedback takes extra time and effort, which typical learners are incentivized to avoid; as a result, AI tutoring often reduces opportunities for genuine independent error-checking and justification.

target: AG2’s claim that AI tutoring inevitably reduces independent thinking
objection: AI tutoring can be designed to show evidence, sources, and uncertainty, and to require learners to verify answers against the underlying materials. With that design, learners are still pushed to evaluate evidence and can practice independent reasoning rather than merely defer to the AI.

target: AG1’s claim that AI tutoring can be made to preserve independent thinking in practice
objection: Even when systems show explanations or sources, many learners still defer to the AI and use it as a shortcut. Because most educational settings reward quick correct answers, verification features do not reliably make students do the independent checking needed to build critical thinking.

target: AG1’s privacy defense that AI can avoid dangerous privacy risks through data minimization and controls
objection: AI systems can infer sensitive traits from ordinary inputs like text, images, or behavior, even when those traits were never explicitly provided. Because this happens through inference and model representations, simple data minimization or access controls do not reliably stop privacy harms.

target: AG2’s claim that AI privacy harms are unavoidable because sensitive attributes can be inferred from model representations
objection: Differential-privacy-style training can place formal limits on how much any individual’s data influences the model, making recovery or inference of sensitive individual attributes statistically unreliable. AI can still provide broad societal benefits while using such privacy-preserving training, so privacy risk is not enough to conclude AI is bad for society.

target: AG1’s claim that differential privacy can substantially reduce inference-based privacy harms in real deployments
objection: Differential-privacy guarantees are fragile in real-world systems because later fine-tuning, personalization, retraining, new data integration, and model updates can invalidate the original privacy budget. Residual leakage through memorization or output-based inference can still expose sensitive traits, so privacy harms remain serious and cannot be reliably prevented in practice.

target: AG2’s claim that later updates undermine the privacy protections of differential privacy
objection: If organizations use DP-aware update procedures and track privacy loss over continued training or fine-tuning, the formal privacy bounds can be preserved over time. Sensitive-attribute disclosure can also be tested with privacy red-teaming, and deployments can be gated or remediated if they fail, so inference-based privacy harms are controllable rather than inevitable.

target: AG1’s assumption that there was no evidence of later retraining or other privacy-budget-bypassing updates
objection: In real deployments, AI systems are commonly fine-tuned, personalized, revised, and updated with new data after release, and organizations are not automatically required to redo DP accounting for every such update. That means the assumption that no such bypass exists is unsupported, and the original privacy guarantees can be undercut.

target: AG2’s claim that inference-based privacy harms are inevitable because they are hard to test and prevent
objection: Sensitive-attribute leakage can be empirically tested with attribute-inference and membership attacks, and deployments can be required to pass thresholds before release. If failures trigger mitigations such as retraining, output restrictions, or feature disablement, dangerous disclosure can be prevented or controlled in practice.

target: AG1’s claim that deployment testing and remediation can reliably control privacy risk
objection: Inference-based disclosure is highly adversary-dependent and the space of possible attacks and contexts is open-ended, so finite tests cannot guarantee safety against future adaptations. Threshold-based gating therefore cannot reliably ensure that dangerous disclosure will not happen, even if the system passes tests under known conditions.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy risks remain dangerous even with layered defenses
objection: Meaningful personal control does not require zero inference leakage; it can be preserved through consent, opt-out, revocation, deletion, and practical remedies. Combined with privacy-preserving training, output restrictions, and ongoing monitoring, layered defenses can reduce privacy risk enough that it is not socially dangerous, while AI still delivers major benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that user-facing governance preserves meaningful control over AI privacy risks
objection: In real-world AI services, users often have only partial, delayed, or hard-to-exercise opt-out and revocation rights, and downstream sharing or inference can defeat those controls across vendors and integrations. Because users lack effective control, residual inference leakage undermines autonomy and safety and remains a serious privacy harm.

target: AG2’s claim that real-world governance cannot preserve meaningful control over personal information
objection: Concrete user-facing controls such as clear consent, opt-out toggles, access to data use, revocation of sharing, and deletion/retention limits can preserve meaningful personal control. With those controls, residual inference leakage does not necessarily defeat autonomy and safety, and AI can still deliver its everyday, educational, accessibility, and safety benefits.
